title: Weeping and shouting (Ezra 3:10–13)
hook: at the new foundation the old weep and others shout, and no one can tell the sounds apart

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cyrus said let him go up, and the exiles started home with the Temple vessels packed for the road. Your line was the ones who go and the ones who send. What did you take one step back toward? Today, they lay a foundation, and the week ends. Day eight hundred seventy-five.

Two sounds rise from the same building site, and they're both loud. The builders have just laid the foundation of the new house of the LORD in Jerusalem. The priests stand in their robes with trumpets. The Levites, sons of Asaph, stand with cymbals. And they sing back and forth, praising and giving thanks, in the King James words, "because he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever toward Israel." The people answer with a great shout. It should be a simple, happy scene. It isn't simple.
screen: `THE FOUNDATION IS LAID.` → `TRUMPETS, CYMBALS, A SONG.` → `A GREAT SHOUT.`

segments.voice: Here's what the text says next: "But many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers, who were ancient men, that had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy." The old men had seen the first Temple. They're standing at the beginning of the second, and they weep. The text doesn't say why. Maybe grief for what was lost. Maybe the memory of what used to stand there. Maybe relief, after so long. Maybe all of it at once. And many others shout for joy at a beginning. Notice who is weeping: not doubters on the edge of the crowd, but priests and Levites, the same groups the text set at the center of the song, along with the heads of families. Then the next line: "So that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people." The text refuses to separate them. It doesn't say the joy drowned out the tears, or that the old men should have cheered up. Both sounds rise together, and the noise, it says, was heard afar off. Anyone listening from a distance heard one sound, made of both.
screen: `THE OLD MEN WEEP.` · `OTHERS SHOUT FOR JOY.` · `NO ONE CAN TELL THE SOUNDS APART.` · then, large: `THE NOISE WAS HEARD AFAR OFF.` · then: `ONE SOUND, MADE OF BOTH.`

segments.voice: Before the bell, a look back at this week. Daniel kept it abroad. Three friends were not alone in the fire. A king was weighed in the balance. Daniel's windows stayed open toward Jerusalem. The wise shine as the firmament. The ones who go, and the ones who send. And today, Asaph's cymbals, weeping and shouting at once. Now the practice: allow mixed feelings. Bring to mind one thing in your life that holds two sounds: a new job and an old one, a child growing up, a move, a loss that also made room. Let both sounds be there. You don't have to choose which one wins. If you pray, you can bring both to God in words from your tradition. The bell holds the time.
Asaph, whose sons the Levites stood with cymbals as the Temple's new foundation was praised with weeping and shouting at once. Today's word.
Your line: weeping and joy together. Today, when one feeling arrives, check gently whether another came with it, and let it stay. Day eight hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: At a Jewish wedding, by tradition, a glass is broken at the end of the ceremony, which some explain as remembering the destruction of Jerusalem even at a moment of great joy.

original.note: Hebrew: weeping, from Ezra 3:13, where the weeping of the people can't be told from the shout of joy.

trapdoor: what you thought: rebuilding the Temple was pure celebration.
what it means: at the new foundation, the old who saw the first house weep, others shout for joy, and the sounds can't be told apart.
what a scholar hears: the text never ranks the two sounds or explains the tears. it lets them rise together, heard afar off.

Possible reasons for the weeping (grief, memory, relief) are offered as 'maybe'; the text gives none.
